clue.text: Serious chap from Spain disposes of heroin for son

indicators.note: to dispose of one thing in exchange for another is to swap a letter out and put a new one in its place

blocks.note: hombre is the Spanish word for a man
H is slang shorthand for heroin
S is the standard abbreviation for son

explanation.surface: A grave Spanish man gets rid of his heroin habit for the sake of his son.
explanation.walkthrough: Swap the H at the front of HOMBRE for S to get SOMBRE.
explanation.definitionFit: Sombre describes a grave, gloomy or solemn manner, a close synonym of serious.

clue.text: Twisted swordplay?

blocks.note: the word is split after its opening letter, leaving word-play behind
a pun is play on words

explanation.walkthrough: Split 'swordplay' as S + wordplay: wordplay is a PUN, so S + PUN gives SPUN. The question mark warns that the word must be broken up.
explanation.definitionFit: Spun is the past participle of spin, so thread that has been spun has been twisted into strands.

clue.text: Arab gentleman raised a very large amount

indicators.note: in a down clue, something raised is lifted upwards, so the letters read from bottom to top

blocks.note: taken as written
fat as in a fat cheque: very large
a sum is an amount of money

explanation.surface: An Arab man has raised a huge sum of money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Raised' seems to be about fundraising, but in a down entry it turns A FAT SUM upside down.
explanation.definitionFit: Mustafa is a common Arabic given name for men, so it stands as an example of an Arab gentleman.

clue.text: Communist agent, one withholding sensitive information

blocks.note: red is the colour long associated with communists
an agent is one who acts, a doer

explanation.surface: A Soviet spy who keeps classified secrets to themselves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Agent' suggests a spy, but here it simply means someone who acts.
explanation.definitionFit: A redactor edits documents, blacking out confidential passages before release, so keeping secret material from readers.

clue.text: Prepared for fighting sea that's rising  …

blocks.note: war is large-scale fighting
the Med is the Mediterranean Sea
something rising is going up

explanation.surface: A navy readies itself for battle as the sea swells.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis links this clue to the next across clue, but each is solved on its own.
explanation.definitionFit: Athletes who have warmed up have done preparatory exercise, so the phrase is an idiom for being ready.

clue.text: Ballpark figure, perhaps, to reset mini-cameras

indicators.note: to reset is to set again in a new order, so the letters get rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written, hyphen dropped

explanation.surface: An estimate of what it costs to reconfigure some small cameras.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ballpark figure' looks like an estimate, but the phrase itself is the example: it comes from US baseball.
explanation.definitionFit: Ballpark figure is a US expression drawn from baseball, so it is one example of a usage peculiar to American English.

clue.text: Choice between meathead and fool? What a mess

indicators.note: the head of a word is its very front, so only its opening letter is kept
something placed between two others sits inside them, flanked on either side

blocks.note: the head of the word meat is its first letter
or is the word that offers a choice
an ass is a fool

explanation.surface: Having to pick between a meathead and a fool: a hopeless situation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Meathead' looks like an insult to sit beside 'fool', but only its head, M, is used.
explanation.definitionFit: A morass is a bog, and figuratively a confused, entangled situation that is hard to escape.

clue.text: Show contempt for facility that makes you sick

definitions.note: a relative clause standing for the noun, a thing that makes you sick

blocks.note: to dis someone is slang for showing them disrespect
facility as in ease of doing something

explanation.surface: Sneering at a place so awful it turns your stomach.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Facility' suggests a building, but it means ease, as in doing something with facility.
explanation.definitionFit: An illness is literally what causes a person to be unwell, so the clause describes it directly.

clue.text: Bill on Ireland coming up later

indicators.note: in a down entry, coming up means travelling upward, so the letters read bottom to top

blocks.note: a bill is a printed notice stuck on a wall
ROI is short for Republic of Ireland

explanation.surface: A piece of legislation on Ireland that is due to come up for debate later.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bill' reads as legislation but is a poster; in a down clue 'on' puts the second piece below it.
explanation.definitionFit: Posterior is a formal word for following in time or order, as opposed to prior.

clue.text: …  couple assist oldest centres to find positive angle

indicators.note: the centre of a word is its middle, so only the middle pair of letters of each word is kept

blocks.note: middle two of six letters
middle two of six letters
middle two of six letters

explanation.surface: Two elderly helpers look for the bright side of things.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis joins this to the previous across clue only for the surface. Each six-letter word yields its middle pair.
explanation.definitionFit: An upside is the favourable aspect of a situation, so it is a synonym of a positive angle.

clue.text: Worries about EU blocking new flower varieties

indicators.note: something blocking a passage sits in the middle of it, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: N is the abbreviation for new
taken as written
roses come in many cultivated varieties

explanation.surface: Gardeners fret that European Union rules will stop new kinds of flowers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Worries about' reads as one phrase, but 'about' is only a link; 'blocking' puts the union between the new and the flowers.
explanation.definitionFit: Neuroses are anxieties or obsessive fears, so the plural noun matches the plural worries.

clue.text: Which state caps recycling? You may soon find out here

definitions.text: You may soon find out here
definitions.note: a sentence describing where news will appear, standing for the stock phrase

indicators.note: recycled material is broken down and remade into something new, so the letters are reformed

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A question about which government limits recycling, with the promise of an answer coming soon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Caps' looks like a verb about limits but is just letters for the mix.
explanation.definitionFit: The stock phrase is a promise that further news will be published in this spot before long.

clue.text: Poor time with those abandoned around harbour  …

indicators.note: abandoned means wild and uninhibited, so the letters run loose in a new order
to be around something is to surround it, enclosing it on both sides

blocks.note: T is the abbreviation for time
taken as written
a haven is a safe harbour

explanation.surface: Destitute people forsaken around a port, having a hard time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poor' at the front looks like an adjective for 'time', but it is the definition, used as a plural noun.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an idiom for people lacking money and possessions, contrasted with the wealthy haves.

clue.text: Cleaner works forever on TV!

definitions.note: a description of the programmes, which run seemingly without end

blocks.note: soap is a cleaning product
opera is the plural of opus, a work, and the word also names musical dramas

explanation.surface: A cleaning lady seems to be endlessly working on television.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cleaner' suggests a person, but it is the cleaning product. The definition is playful: long-running serials seem never to end.
explanation.definitionFit: Television serial dramas such as long-running daily series often continue for decades, which is the joke behind the description.

clue.text: …  confused and drained, after being told to leave

indicators.note: coming after something means following it, which fixes the order the two parts are joined in

blocks.note: scram is a curt order to go away
drained of blood, as in bled dry

explanation.surface: Someone left bewildered and exhausted after being thrown out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Told to leave' is the command SCRAM, which goes first since 'drained' comes after it.
explanation.definitionFit: A scrambled mind or message is muddled and jumbled, so it is a synonym of confused.

clue.text: Young energetic type is originally hard to find

indicators.note: originally means at the origin or start, so only the opening letters are kept

blocks.note: first letter
first letter
first letter
first letter

explanation.surface: A lively youngster is elusive.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is an adjective phrase standing for a creature that is famously elusive.
explanation.definitionFit: The yeti is the legendary Himalayan snowman, so elusive that no reliable sighting has ever been recorded.

clue.text: Ideal condition for teenagers rarely applies to their rooms

blocks.note: first meaning: a complexion free of pimples, which teenagers long for
second meaning: perfectly clean, which teenage bedrooms seldom are

explanation.walkthrough: The same word describes clear skin and a scrupulously tidy room; the surface is a gentle dig at teenage untidiness.
explanation.definitionFit: Spots are pimples on skin and also marks of dirt, so the adjective covers both a clear complexion and immaculate cleanliness.

clue.text: Way to torture supporter, having lost bet

indicators.note: something lost is no longer there, so those letters drop out

blocks.note: a bracket is a support fixed to a wall to hold a shelf
taken as written; these letters are scattered through the first word

explanation.surface: A cruel method of tormenting a fan who has just lost a wager.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove B, E and T from BRACKET and RACK is left.
explanation.definitionFit: The rack was a medieval frame used to stretch victims' bodies, a historic instrument of torture.

clue.text: Depressed liberal leaves assembly

indicators.note: one who leaves departs, so that letter is taken out

blocks.note: a conclave is a private assembly, such as the one that elects a pope
L is the abbreviation for liberal

explanation.surface: A dejected Liberal walks out of a meeting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Depressed' reads as gloomy, but the answer means physically pressed in.
explanation.definitionFit: A concave surface curves inward like a hollow, so it is depressed in the physical sense.

clue.text: Prime Paris renovation is developed underground

definitions.note: a description of a potato, which grows in the soil

indicators.note: renovation means remodelling, so the letters are rebuilt in a fresh order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A top-quality Paris building project is built below ground level.
explanation.walkthrough: Maris Piper is a popular British variety of potato; the definition describes it as a tuber grown in soil.
explanation.definitionFit: Potatoes are tubers that swell beneath the soil, so this named variety grows below the surface.

clue.text: Unadulterated passage read out? That's just childish

indicators.note: reading words out means saying them, so the answer matches their spoken form

blocks.note: unadulterated means pure and a passage between seats is an aisle

explanation.surface: Someone reading a pure text aloud is mocked as babyish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Passage' suggests a piece of text to be read, but it is a corridor between rows.
explanation.definitionFit: Puerile comes from Latin puer, a boy, and describes silly, immature behaviour.

clue.text: Plant supervisor reloads component

indicators.note: a component is one part of a larger whole, so the answer is a part of the words before it

blocks.note: spans the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: A factory manager puts parts back into a machine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plant' looks like a factory with its supervisor, but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Sorrel is a leafy herb with a sharp lemony taste, so it is an example of a plant.

clue.text: Display of determination to take care of surplus material

blocks.note: to mind children is to look after them
anything over is left over, surplus
matter is physical material

explanation.surface: Someone shows real resolve in dealing with leftover stuff.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as tidying leftovers; each word in the wordplay is a plain synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom names willpower overcoming physical limits, as when sheer resolve conquers pain or difficulty.

clue.text: Make fast arrest — it may be filed

blocks.note: first meaning: to fasten with a metal pin
second meaning: to catch a criminal
third meaning: a fingernail, which is shaped with a file

explanation.walkthrough: Three meanings in a row; 'filed' suggests paperwork about an arrest, but it is a nail file.
explanation.definitionFit: The word works as a verb for fastening and for catching a suspect, and as a noun for the horny tip of a finger.

clue.text: Floored a criminal with what protects many churches

indicators.note: something criminal is crooked and wrong, so the letters are bent out of their order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A burglar is knocked down while stealing from churches.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface hints at metal theft from churches, a real problem in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: Many old churches are covered with sheets of metal, which keep rain out of the building beneath.

clue.text: Roman queen overturns a country in Africa

indicators.note: to overturn is to flip upside down, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: taken as written
Niger is a West African country

explanation.surface: A Roman queen topples an African nation.
explanation.walkthrough: Regina is Latin for queen, hence 'Roman'; it is also the R in British royal signatures.
explanation.definitionFit: Regina was the word for queen in Latin, the language of ancient Rome.

clue.text: One seeking satisfaction coming with large inventory  …

blocks.note: something due is expected, coming
L is the abbreviation for large
an inventory is a list of items

explanation.surface: A shopper hoping for fulfilment arrives with a long list of goods.
explanation.walkthrough: To 'demand satisfaction' was the old formula for challenging someone to a duel over an insult.
explanation.definitionFit: Insulted gentlemen once sought satisfaction for their honour by fighting with swords or pistols.

clue.text: …  including a balloon!

definitions.note: a preposition standing for an adverb meaning also

blocks.note: taken as written
to balloon is to swell up

explanation.surface: Continuing the previous clue: the long inventory has a balloon on it too.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Balloon' looks like a noun on the list, but it is a verb meaning to grow larger.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means too or in addition, which is the sense of including something in a list.
